In ''geol.'', a type of reversed fault where, as the result of enormous tangential pressure, the rocks on the upper side of the fault have been pushed or thrust for a greater or less distance, with an entire severance of continuity, over the underlying masses. The line of junction of the dissevered parts in such cases is denominated a ''thrust-plane.''

{{RunningHeader|thrust|6318|thug}}1. To push forcibly; shove; force: as, to ''thrust'' a hand into one's pocket, or one's feet into slippers; to ''thrust'' a stick into the sand: usually followed by ''from'', ''in'', ''off'', ''away'', or other adverb or preposition. {{smaller block|Sotilly this lettre doun she ''threste'' ''Under'' his pilwe. {{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant's Tale, l. 759.}}}} {{smaller block|Gehazi came near to ''thrust'' her ''away''. {{right|2 Ki. iv. 27.}}}} {{smaller block|Neither shall one ''thrust'' another. {{right|Joel ii. 8.}}}} {{smaller block|He ''thrusts'' you ''from'' his love, she pulls thee on. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, iii. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|At this some of them laughed at me, some called me fool, and some began to ''thrust'' me ''about''. {{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim's Progress, ii.}}}} {{smaller block|Near the bed of the brook is a stone on which they shew the print of his [Christ's] feet, supposed to be made as they were ''thrusting'' him ''along''. {{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. i. 22.}}}} 2. Figuratively, to drive; force; compel. {{smaller block|And into the concession of this Bellarmine is ''thrust'' by the force of our argument. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Real Presence, iv. 8.}}}} 3†. To press; pack; jam. {{smaller block|Two & thretty thried shippes ''thrast'' full of pepull. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4129.}}}} {{smaller block|A hall ''thrust'' full of bare heads, some bald, some bush'd, Some bravely branch'd. {{right|''Tomkis'' (?), Albumazar, i. 3.}}}} 4. To stab; pierce. {{smaller block|A base Walloon, to win the Dauphin's grace, ''Thrust'' Talbot with a spear into the back. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., i. 1. 138.}}}} '''To thrust aside''', to push or jostle out of the way; displace. {{smaller block|There are few Venetian memorials to be seen in these towns; and if the winged lion ever appeared over their gates he has been carefully ''thrust aside'' by kings and emperors. {{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 292.}}}} '''To thrust forth.''' (''a'') To drive out; expel: as, she was ''thrust forth'' into the storm. (''b'') To protrude; cause to project. {{smaller block|From S. Michael's Mount Southward, immediately there is ''thrust forth'' a biland or demi-isle. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Camden, p. 189.}}}} '''To thrust on.''' (''a'') To impel; urge. {{smaller block|Did she not ''thrust'' me ''on'', And to my duty clapt the spur of honour? {{right|''Fletcher'', Double Marriage, iv. 3.}}}} (''b'') To push forward; advance, in space or time. {{smaller block|This [evidence] ''thrusts on'' the building of the upper and greater church to a later time, surely not earlier than the reign of Justinian. {{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 169.}}}} '''To thrust one's nose into.''' See ''nose''1.—'''To thrust one's self in''' or '''into''', to obtrude; intrude; enter where one is not welcome. {{smaller block|Who 's there, I say? How dare you ''thrust yourselves'' ''Into'' my private meditations? {{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., ii. 2. 65.}}}} '''To thrust out.''' (''a'') To drive out; expel. {{smaller block|They were ''thrust out'' of Egypt. {{right|Ex. xii. 39.}}}} (''b'') To stick out; protrude. {{smaller block|He spent some three minutes in ''thrusting out'' his tongue at me as far as he could without damaging the roots. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, i.}}}} (''c'') To force out. {{smaller block|The anguish of my soul ''thrusts out'' this truth, You are a tyrant. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid's Tragedy, iii. 1.}}}} '''To thrust through''', to pierce from side to side; transfix. {{smaller block|Laeca Mariam, solicitous only for the king's safety, charging furiously every one that approached, was ''thrust through'' with a lance by a common soldier, who had approached him unobserved. {{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, II. 250.}}}} '''To thrust together''', to compress. {{smaller block|He ''thrust'' the fleece ''together''. {{right|Judges vi. 38.}}}} '''To thrust upon''', to force upon; impose or inflict upon. {{smaller block|Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness ''thrust upon'' 'em. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 5. 158.}}}} {{smaller block|='''Syn. 1.''' ''Thrust'' is stronger, more energetic, than ''push'' or ''drive'', and represents a more dignified act than ''shove''. No other distinction really exists among these words.}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To push or drive with or as with a pointed weapon. {{smaller block|He next his falchion tried in closer fight; But the keen falchion had no power to bite; He ''thrust'', the blunted point returned again. {{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Ovid's Metamorph., xii. 643.}}}} {{smaller block|They do not ''thrust'' with the skill of fencers, but cut up with the barbarity of butchers. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 422.}}}} '''2.''' To push one's self; force a way or passage. {{smaller block|Then he ''threste'' thourgh the presse to that Saisne, and for to yeve hym a grete stroke he reysed his ax. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 199.}}}} {{smaller block|My fair reputation, If I ''thrust'' into crowds and seek occasions, Suffers opinion. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, ii. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Fish . . . ''thrust'' up little brooks to spawn. {{right|''W. Lawson'' (Arber's Eng. Garner, I. 197).}}}} '''3.''' To crowd, or assemble in crowds; press in; throng. {{smaller block|Young, old, ''thrust'' there In mighty concourse. {{right|''Chapman'', Odyssey. (''Johnson.'')}}}} '''4†.''' To rush; make a dash. {{smaller block|As doth an eager hound ''thrust'' to a hind. {{right|''Spenser.''}}}} '''thrust'''1 (thrust), ''n.'' [< ''thrust''1, ''v.''] '''1.''' A violent push or drive, as with a pointed weapon pushed in the direction of its length, or with the hand or foot, or with an instrument; a stab; as a term of fence, in general, any attack by a fencer with a point. {{smaller|With reference to the saber, broadsword, and other cut-and-thrust weapons, it distinguishes the use of the point from a blow or cut, and is less important than in small-sword and foil work, where the point alone is used. In fencing thrusts are always made by extending the arm before moving the foot or body.}} {{smaller block|A ''thrust'' (quoth he) of a sword, which went in at his side. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 71. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}} {{smaller block|Lieut. Felton, being behind, made a ''Thrust'' with a common Tenpenny Knife over Fryer's Arm at the Duke, which lighted so fatally that he slit his Heart in two, leaving the Knife sticking in the Body. {{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 7.}}}} {{smaller block|I have heard Gentlemen say, Sister, that one shou'd take great Care, when one makes a ''Thrust'' in Fencing, not to lye open ones self. {{right|''Congreve'', Love for Love, ii. 9.}}}} '''2.''' Attack; assault. {{smaller block|There is one ''thrust'' at your pure, pretended mechanism. {{right|''Dr. H. More'', Divine Dialogues.}}}} '''3.''' In ''mech.'', the stress which acts between two contiguous bodies, or parts of a body, when each pushes the other from itself. {{smaller|A thrust tends}} T {{smaller block|to compress or shorten each body on which it acts in the direction of its action.}} [[File:century v08 p0122 c2f1.png|center|289px]] {{c|Thrust in Medieval Pointed Vaulting.}} {{c|The section in plan is taken at the level of the head of the flying-buttress. The arrows indicate the directions of the thrusts.}} 4. In ''coal-mining'', a crushing of the pillars caused by excess of weight of the superincumbent rocks, the floor being harder than the roof. {{smaller block|It is nearly the same as ''creep'', except that in the latter the workings are disorganized by the upheaval of the floor, which, being softer than the roof, is first to yield to the pressure.}} 5. The white whey which is the last to leave the curd under pressure. ''E. H. Knight.''—{{smaller|'''Line of thrust.''' If a straight line be drawn through each bed-joint in the ring of an arch so as to represent the position and direction of the resultant pressure at that joint, a curve drawn so as to touch each of these lines at its intersection with the joint from which it is derived is the line of thrust of the arch. If the arch is stable its line of thrust must lie within the middle third of the depth of the arch-ring.—'''Thrust of an arch,''' the force exerted in an outward direction by an arch, and explained by considering its separate stones or voussoirs as so many wedges. Its tendency is to overturn the abutments or walls from which the arch springs, and to deform and ultimately destroy the arch by causing it to break and rise at its haunches. Hence all arches require to be secured in some way against this force, as by the mass of the abutments (the Roman method), by a system of buttresses (the medieval method), or by ties (the Italian method). Also called ''push of an arch.''}} ¶ '''thrust2''', ''n.'' An obsolete or dialectal form of ''thirst.'' '''thrust3''' (thrust), ''n.'' See ''thurse'' and ''thrush''3. To drive with impetuosity. ''Ramsay.'' (''Jamieson.'') [Scotch.] '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To emit a low, dull sound such as is produced by a blow upon a comparatively soft substance. {{smaller block|He felt the hollow-beaten mosses ''thud''
And tremble.{{right|''Tennyson'', Balin and Balan.}}}} '''2.''' To rush with a hollow sound. ''Gavin Douglas'', tr. of Virgil, p. 422. (''Jamieson.'') [Scotch.]—'''3.'''
